reasons: Lake identity confirms case_name Townsend v. Sain, court U.S. Supreme Court, date_decided 1963-03-18, and year 1963.
Lake citations confirm official cite 372 U.S. 293, parallel cites 83 S. Ct. 745 and 9 L. Ed. 2d 770, and vendor citation 1963 U.S. LEXIS 1941.
The opinion states that if a person's will was overborne or the confession was not the product of a rational intellect and free will, the confession is inadmissible because coerced.
The opinion expressly applies those standards to drug-induced statements and says questioning that in fact produces a confession not the product of a free intellect renders it inadmissible.
The opinion states that it is not significant that the drug was administered and questions asked by persons unfamiliar with hyoscine's truth-serum properties, if those properties exist.
Footnote 5 supports the reliability point: whether scopolamine produces true or false confessions, statements caused by it were constitutionally inadmissible.
residual_risks: The Court made no finding on scopolamine's medical properties or whether the administered dose actually caused Townsend's confessions; it remanded for factfinding.
reviewed.suggested_tightening: To avoid overread, phrase the holding as conditional: if the drug in fact had truth-serum properties and caused the statements.
